name: Stockport to Manchester Piccadilly
note: Corridor waypoints and station positions from an OpenStreetMap export (tools/osm-to-network.mjs, 8 October 2026): the shortest rail path from Davenport to Piccadilly, resampled every 60 m, on one track of the four-track line, with the Hazel Grove line (11 October 2026, the same way) put in front of it from 400 m beyond Hazel Grove, so the line runs on past the last platform. Landmarks are still by hand. Each station's access (its car park's and bus link's pools beyond a walk) is from tools/census-to-network.mjs (12 October 2026): straight-line distances from Census 2021 Output Areas times a road factor of 1.3, at 8 m/s driving and 5 m/s by bus, half of each area's residents driving and half by bus (docs/DESIGN.md, Homes and draw, Pools); the car parks' spaces and the stages' prices are game choices.

tracks.use: the Hazel Grove line towards Stockport
the Hazel Grove line towards Hazel Grove

trackNote: Offsets are where each track runs across the corridor, 1.25 times the real spacing from the OpenStreetMap tracks so the trains, drawn 1.3 times real width, pass clear of each other. On the open line the corridor follows the westmost track. The layout list moves the tracks where the corridor follows another track and around the stations; they ease between layouts over `ease` metres.

layout.note: The stopper turns round in platform 4, so both its tracks run into it; the fast lines take platforms 3 and 2 either side of the two wide islands.
The Hazel Grove line turns round in platform 1, crossing over the main lines on the way in; it eases over a longer run as it has further to go.

South of Stockport the corridor follows the two-track Hazel Grove line; the four main lines start here on top of it, as if the Crewe pair had just joined at Edgeley, and spread out towards the station.
From the crossover north of the viaduct to Slade Lane junction the corridor follows the second track from the west. Heaton Chapel and Levenshulme are in this stretch.
Through Hazel Grove the corridor follows the eastern track; it crosses to the western one north of the platforms.
The stopper turns round in platform 5, so both its tracks run into it; the expresses come into platform 6 alongside.

landmarks.name: Stockport Viaduct
landmarks.note: 27 arches on tall piers, about 34 m over the Mersey, red brick; built 1839-40 by George Watson Buck and widened on its west side to four tracks in 1887-89, the join showing down the soffits (geograph 1073460, 8038086; Commons: Category:Stockport Viaduct). Floodlit at night. Its span along the line is where the Environment Agency's LIDAR has the ground fall away beneath it (tools/lidar-to-terrain.mjs).

landmarks.name: River Mersey
landmarks.note: Where the LIDAR has the valley floor lowest under the viaduct.

landmarks.name: M60
landmarks.note: Where the LIDAR has the motorway's level stretch under the viaduct, north of the river.

landmarks.name: Stockport Pyramid
landmarks.note: Steel-framed blue glass pyramid of 1987-92 by Michael Hyde and Associates, beside the M60 at Brinksway (geograph 2350452, 3116288; Commons: Category:Stockport Pyramid gives 53.408, -2.1754). At the real spot; its size from the photos, not survey.

landmarks.name: The Plaza
landmarks.note: The 1932 art deco super cinema on Mersey Square: a tall cream faience front with a stepped centre and its name down a fin, built into the sandstone cliff (geograph 1974759, 5194359). At its real spot, facing the river. Proportions from the photos.

landmarks.name: Merseyway
landmarks.note: The 1960s shopping precinct built on a deck over the River Mersey, two runs of shops either side of the walk (geograph 7305032, 8287347; at its real spot, about 53.4114, -2.1600). Stands on the river as the map draws it, straight out from the viaduct, between it and the A6's Wellington Bridge; the shops' sizes from memory.

landmarks.note: Red sandstone parish church on the Market Place, its tower at the west end (Commons: Category:St Mary's Church, Stockport gives 53.411234, -2.155514). At the real spot, across the A6 from Merseyway; size from memory.

platformNote: Which platform each service uses (12 October 2026). The owner: trains from Stockport to Manchester use platforms 3 and 4, both of them. Wikipedia (Stockport railway station, Manchester Piccadilly station, read 12 October 2026): at Stockport platform 4 is the northbound stoppers', 3 the northbound main-line trains (Avanti West Coast, 3 an hour, and CrossCountry, 2 an hour, to Piccadilly), 2 the southbound main-line trains (to London, Bristol and Bournemouth), 1 southbound stoppers and signalled for trains to Manchester, 0 southbound towards Hazel Grove and Buxton, 3a the weekly train to Stalybridge; at Piccadilly platform 1 is on the north side (the kit's +v) and 13 and 14 on the south, 5 to 9 are the longest and mostly Avanti's and CrossCountry's, 10 to 12 shorter, for local trains including the Buxton line. Game choices: the stopper turns at Stockport in 4, 3 and the bay 0, and at Piccadilly in 5, 11, 12 and 4, each unit its own first choice so every platform built has trains; the Hazel Grove line turns in Stockport's 1; the expresses use 3 north and 2 south at Stockport (running through until those are built) and 6 and 7 at Piccadilly (5 while the player owns it without the shed). A through station's platforms are the halt's (1) and the second platform (2), which aren't their real numbers everywhere. The expresses' destinations south: Avanti's London Euston, CrossCountry's Bristol Temple Meads (some go to Bournemouth); one of each every 1,200 sim seconds (two clock hours), not their real frequency, which the clock running six times faster would make a train every few minutes.
roadNote: Roads between neighbouring stations, for the rail replacement buses (and later trams and buses): from memory, 12 October 2026, since OpenStreetMap couldn't be reached from the session that drew them. Each follows the real main road, mostly the A6, which runs beside the line all the way, with the side streets to each station; corners are approximate to tens of metres. tools/osm-to-roads.mjs redraws them from an OpenStreetMap export.
